articles.title: EXTRAS'S EXTRAS
articles.summary: This 'EXTRAS'S EXTRAS' column highlights concerns over the astronomical future of Fremont Peak following Ranger Rick Morales' retirement and an unclear administrative transition, with a March FPOA meeting planned to discuss these issues. It also previews an upcoming SJAA meeting with member presentations, including on the Ephemeris, and a Beginning Astronomy Class on binocular astronomy by Jay Freeman.

articles.title: FEBRUARY
articles.summary: This document outlines the schedule of astronomy-related events for February, featuring multiple star parties at locations like Houge Park and Fremont Peak. It also includes a general meeting, an open board meeting, and a beginning astronomy class focused on using binoculars. Key astronomical details like sunset, moonset, and moonrise times are provided for some dates.

articles.title: MARCH
articles.summary: This document outlines the San Jose Astronomical Association's (SJAA) schedule for March, featuring several star parties at Houge Park and Fremont Peak. The month also includes a 'Telescope Types and Mounts' astronomy class and a general meeting where Don Machholz will discuss the Messier Marathon. An important note reminds attendees about SJAA insurance covering members at sponsored events.

articles.title: LOST IN A NORTHERN LIBRATION
articles.summary: On December 13, 1997, Akkana Peck took advantage of a clear night and good northern and eastern libration to observe the far-northern regions of the Moon using a 4.5" reflector. Peck focused on identifying features near the north pole, noting Anaxagoras and its ray system, Mare Humboldtianum, and challenges in lunar identification due to insufficient atlas detail. The article describes the author's visual experience and reliance on different references for feature identification.

articles.title: Jay Freeman
articles.summary: The author recounts a challenging but rewarding multi-night observing trip to a friend's private observatory in Bear Valley, Sierra Nevada foothills, after Christmas. Despite cold temperatures and getting lost, they enjoyed exceptionally dark skies, focusing on observing numerous faint Herschel objects with various telescopes. The report details the equipment used, specific deep-sky targets, and the general experience of amateur astronomy under pristine conditions.

articles.title: Mark Taylor
articles.summary: Mark Taylor describes an impromptu, highly successful observing session at Fremont Peak on December 19, prompted by an unexpected clear weather forecast amidst a busy schedule. Despite initial challenges with site access and minor light interference, he made detailed observations of Jupiter, Saturn (noting exceptional seeing conditions), M42, M37, and the Pleiades, and even caught a meteor. The night also included interactions with fellow stargazers, concluding as haze and a breeze began to roll in.

articles.title: Diary, from p. 3
articles.summary: The observer documented an evening of stargazing, starting with galaxies and the Beehive, followed by a vivid moonrise and two distinct green meteor sightings near Orion and Sirius. Despite some horizon obstruction, seeing conditions were exceptionally good, as confirmed by stable diffraction rings around Sirius. The session concluded early due to increasing cloud cover and atmospheric moisture.

articles.title: RETRO-ASTRONOMY
articles.summary: The author, John Gleason, details a challenging December 26th observing trip to Fremont Peak State Park, where a locked gate forced him to set up at Coulter camp. Intending to test equipment for an upcoming Australia trip alongside fellow observer Dave Cooper, their peaceful, cold-weather session was unexpectedly interrupted by other campers' loud music. This disruption prompted Gleason to reflect on the early days of amateur astronomy in the 1960s and 70s.

articles.title: Extras, from p. 1
articles.summary: The article describes a peculiar stargazing event organized in Northern California for the Quadrantids meteor shower, inviting participants to observe from warm, clothing-optional mineral springs. The author humorously questions the practicalities and social etiquette of such an arrangement, highlighting its many comical aspects rather than providing an actual observing report.

articles.title: Jim Van Nuland
articles.summary: This article details a successful rescheduled stargazing event at Christopher School on December 15th, featuring four telescopes. Approximately 30 GATE and 4th-grade students observed Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn, despite some high haze and later clouds. The event provided an interactive learning experience, allowing students to engage with telescopes and celestial objects.

articles.title: Lost, from p. 1
articles.summary: An observer details their challenging experience identifying a specific crater on the Moon's limb, using a 'crater-hopping' method. They struggled with the foreshortening shown on charts and found a lunar globe significantly more useful for accurate orientation and identification. The observer eventually deduced the target crater was likely Hermite, located past the north pole, after initially misidentifying it.

articles.title: Retro-Astronomy, from p. 4
articles.summary: The author reminisces about classic astronomy equipment while contrasting it with modern gear, recounting an observing session featuring a 4-inch F9 fluorite telescope that provided exceptional views of M42 and other deep-sky objects. Despite issues with an SBIG autoguider due to cold temperatures, the session included a positive comparison of the fluorite scope's sharpness to a Traveler telescope. The article captures the blend of nostalgia and appreciation for current astronomical technology.

articles.title: Mark J. Wagner
articles.summary: Mark J. Wagner recounts a winter solstice observing session at Fremont Peak, detailing the distinct experience of cold-weather astronomy, including the scenic drive, specific challenges, and the camaraderie among fellow observers. Despite the chilly conditions, he and his partners engaged in public outreach, showing planets to a family, before proceeding with their deep-sky object hunt, appreciating the tranquil yet rugged nature of winter observing.

articles.title: Cold Skies
articles.summary: The article describes an amateur astronomer's deep-sky observing session with a companion, primarily hunting galaxies in Cetus and Eridanus, emphasizing the reward of manual star-hopping. While initially successful in finding numerous challenging objects, observing conditions unexpectedly deteriorated on the winter solstice of 1997, leading them to conclude their session despite extensive preparations for the cold. The author reflects on the personal skill development gained through traditional astronomical navigation.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article provides an observing guide for the month, highlighting the Moon's high elevation and favorable librations for viewing northern and eastern maria, especially between the third and seventh. It suggests specific lunar features to observe and mentions a lunar eclipse on the 26th that won't be visible. Brief notes on other planets, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, are also included.

articles.title: Jay Freeman
articles.summary: Jay Freeman details several astronomical observing sessions, including deep-sky observations with a 5-inch refractor from Fremont Peak and successful backyard astronomy using an 80mm refractor in a suburban setting. He demonstrates that interesting results, such as spotting faint galaxies or Messier objects, are achievable with modest equipment. Additionally, the article briefly touches upon mail-order transaction challenges and reviews "Burnham's Celestial Handbook."

articles.title: Don Machholz
articles.summary: This article, titled "Don Machholz," provides updates on comet observations and discoveries, highlighting 1997 as the "Year of Comet Hale-Bopp" while mentioning other visible comets. It also serves as a personal update from Don Machholz, directing readers to his *Comet Comments* newsletter and two websites for comet information, positions, and his comet hunting program. Additionally, it features "Comet Hunting Notes," emphasizing the significant contributions of amateur astronomers, particularly those using refractor telescopes, to comet discoveries.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: This document provides detailed orbital elements for four comets: Hale-Bopp, Meunier-Dupouy, Tempel-Tuttle, and Hartley 2, including their perihelion dates and distances, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period. Additionally, it offers ephemeris data for each comet for January to March 1998, listing their Right Ascension, Declination, Elongation, Sky position, and expected Magnitude, useful for observational planning.

articles.title: Lunar Phases
articles.summary: This document provides a schedule of lunar phases, including First Quarter, Full Moon, Last Quarter, and New Moon, for a specific period. For each phase, it lists the exact time and date (PST), along with the moon's rise, transit, and set times, enabling observers to track the moon's position.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for the planet Mercury, listing its astronomical data for three specific dates (likely within a month). It includes the planet's rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension, magnitude, and declination, serving as a guide for observers.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This article provides an ephemeris for the planet Venus, detailing its astronomical magnitude, distance from the Sun, and daily rise, transit, and set times. It also lists Venus's right ascension and declination for three specific dates within a month, serving as a guide for its observable position.

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Mars, detailing its magnitude, distance in A.U., and daily rise, transit, and set times. It also lists the planet's right ascension and declination for several specific dates, serving as a practical guide for observers.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Jupiter, listing its magnitude and distance from the Sun. It includes a table with rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination for three specific dates in the month.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document presents an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Saturn, detailing its apparent magnitude (+1.0) and approximate distance (9:97 A.U.). It provides daily rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension and declination for the 7th, 17th, and 27th of an unspecified month. This data is essential for observers to locate and track Saturn in the night sky.

articles.title: SOL Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?
articles.summary: The document, titled "SOL Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?", presents a table of astronomical data relevant to a G2V star system, implicitly referring to our Sun. It includes values for Hours of Darkness (HOD), rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension (R.A.) and Declination (Dec.) for several specific dates. Despite the title's provocative question, the content is solely a tabular display of celestial mechanics.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document presents a tabular listing of begin and end times for astronomical twilight on specific dates, identified by Julian Date. It provides essential data for observers to determine periods of optimal sky darkness for astronomical activities in both the morning and evening.

articles.title: Siderealtime
articles.summary: This document presents a concise table detailing the transit right ascension at local midnight for three specific points in time, likely days of a month. It provides corresponding sidereal time values, such as 09:01, 09:40, and 10:20, for these measurements. The data serves as a quick reference for sidereal time calculations.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night
articles.summary: The article titled "Darkest Saturday Night" provides astronomical timings for February 28, 1998. It lists the sunset, end of twilight, moonset, and beginning of dawn, indicating key periods of darkness suitable for night sky observation.

articles.title: ACTIVITIES THROUGH OTHER CLUBS
articles.summary: The article details various astronomical activities organized by TAC and PAS. TAC hosts regular Wednesday star parties at Montebello and mobile first-quarter Friday star parties, along with third-quarter Friday events at Van Meter School. PAS offers public viewing at Foothill Observatory every clear Friday evening and solar viewing every clear Saturday morning, encouraging participation from SJAA members.

articles.title: February
articles.summary: The document outlines the schedule for February, including three key events. These events are a PAS General Meeting on the 13th featuring a presentation on "Project Phoenix And SETI," a PAS Board Meeting on the 18th at Foothill Observatory, and an HVAG Starparty at Grant Ranch on the 28th.

articles.title: March
articles.summary: The document outlines the Pasadena Astronomical Society's (PAS) activities for March, including a General Meeting ("Member's Night") on the 13th and a Board Meeting on the 18th at Foothill Observatory. It also notes a HVAG star party scheduled for the 28th at Grant Ranch.

articles.title: Shallow Sky, from p. 7
articles.summary: The article offers current astronomical viewing recommendations, including looking for meteor showers and checking less famous comets. It highlights Venus at its brightest around February 19, emphasizing strict solar safety for any daytime viewing. Furthermore, it advises monitoring increased solar activity and spectacular sunspots, suggesting the use of solar filters and participation in local solar observation sessions.

articles.title: SUBMIT
articles.summary: This document encourages members to submit articles for publication in the *SJAA Ephemeris* newsletter. Submissions should be sent via email to Dave North at Timocharis@aol.com, with a deadline of the tenth of each month for inclusion in the following month's issue. Authors are requested to include their name and phone number with their article.

articles.title: PERIODICAL PUBLICATION STATEMENT
articles.summary: This document is a periodical publication statement for the "SJAA Ephemeris," the monthly newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It specifies that the newsletter is published 12 times a year, from January through December, and provides the association's address. The statement is dated February 1998.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors for an organization, including their names and contact phone numbers. It identifies key roles such as President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and several Directors.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document details the staff and key personnel for the "Ephemeris" publication and associated organizational programs. It provides contact information for roles like editor, circulation, layout, and proof, alongside chairpersons and teachers for activities, mentoring, observational astronomy, observatory, school star parties, and the telescope loaner program.

articles.title: Current Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists telescopes currently on loan, along with the borrower's name and the due date for each instrument. It states that individuals interested in borrowing a scope will be added to a waiting list until it becomes available after its return date.

articles.title: Extended Scope Loans
articles.summary: The document, "Extended Scope Loans," lists various telescopes that have had their loan periods extended, some indefinitely, and are currently with specific borrowers. It also outlines a process for interested individuals to request borrowing one of these scopes, which involves coordinating a reasonable transfer time with the current borrower.

articles.title: Available Scopes
articles.summary: The article lists several telescopes, including Dobsons, a refractor, and a Newtonian, that are immediately available for loan to SJAA members. These scopes are stored at various members' homes, and interested individuals can contact Mike Koop for pickup arrangements at SJAA events.

articles.title: Waiting List
articles.summary: This article, from the February 1998 SJAA Ephemeris, outlines a waiting list for club telescopes, noting that one 8" Celestron S/C scope is currently undergoing repairs to its secondary mirror, with completion expected in February. It provides contact information for members to reserve scopes and makes a request for members who might have space to store equipment.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing options for new or renewal memberships at $15 for regular members and $6 for juniors. Members can also add a Sky & Telescope subscription for an additional $27. The form provides instructions for submitting payment via check and includes contact information for the treasurer and the organization.
